A hands-on setup guide — PowerShell and the Claude desktop app — plus every error I hit along the way

I kept reading that OutSystems now ships an MCP server — for both O11 and ODC — so an AI assistant like Claude can read your apps and build in them. I wanted to see that for myself.

So one evening, purely out of curiosity, I set it up from scratch. I’m an OutSystems developer, not a terminal person: I opened PowerShell, worked through the official docs — and promptly hit eight different errors.

This post is the guide I wish I’d had: what MCP actually is, how the setup differs between OutSystems 11 and ODC, the exact commands for both PowerShell and the Claude desktop app, and the one-line fix for every error I met.

TL;DR
  • O11: the MCP server runs inside Service Studio on your PC. Install Claude Code, install the skill, click Start MCP Server, run one claude mcp add command.
  • ODC: the MCP server is hosted by OutSystems. Install one plugin with your tenant name and sign in through the browser.
  • Desktop app: O11 works in a local Code session; ODC works everywhere via a small proxy called mcp-remote.
  • Expect about 20 minutes for O11 and 10 for ODC.

Why does OutSystems MCP exist?

Before the how, the why. Low-code made building fast — but a lot of our day still goes into work around the building:

  • Understanding what’s already there. Opening a five-year-old module and working out what it does, what depends on it, and what breaks if you touch an action.
  • Writing things down. Documentation, onboarding notes and impact analyses that nobody has time for.
  • Repetitive scaffolding. The same entities, list screens, CRUD actions and validations, app after app.
  • Context switching. Requirements in Jira, designs in Figma, specs in Drive — and the app in Service Studio or ODC Portal, with you copy-pasting between them.
  • Release chores (ODC). Checking what’s deployed where, running impact checks, promoting between stages, digging through logs after something fails.

OutSystems’ answer is to open the platform to the AI coding assistants developers already use. MCP is the standard plug that makes that possible: your assistant gets real, typed access to your application model instead of guessing from screenshots.

What that gives you

  • Answers about your own apps, in seconds. “Walk me through this module”, “what calls this action?”, “which apps are in QA?” — read from the live model, not from memory.
  • Real changes, not code to copy. Claude creates entities, screens and logic directly in your module (O11) or through Mentor (ODC).
  • One assistant across your tools. The same Claude that reads your Jira story and Figma design can build the feature in OutSystems — no copy-paste in between.
  • Evolve in place. For O11 especially: modernise an estate you already run, without a migration or replatform.
  • Same governance. Every change still goes through the OutSystems lifecycle: Compare-and-Merge review in O11; your ODC roles, confirmations and audit trail in ODC.
  • Your choice of assistant. It’s an open standard — OutSystems supports Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Kiro, Codex and more.

What it isn’t

It isn’t autopilot. O11 model writes are still Beta, results need review, and screens are less reliable than data and logic. Think of it as a fast, tireless pair programmer — you stay the one who accepts, publishes and deploys.

First, what is MCP?

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets an AI assistant use tools in other apps. Think of it as a USB port for AI: the app exposes a set of tools (“list entities”, “create a screen”, “publish”), and any MCP-compatible assistant can plug in and use them.

OutSystems now ships an MCP server for both platforms. Claude is the assistant on the other end.

The key thing to understand before you start: the two platforms connect in completely different ways.

That one difference explains almost every other one:

What you need

  • Windows 10/11 and a Claude account that includes Claude Code
  • For O11: Service Studio 11.55.91 or later, and a dev/test module you own
  • For ODC: your tenant hostname (e.g. acme.outsystems.dev) and the ODC roles for what you want Claude to do (Asset management → Create/Change, Release management → Deploy assets)
💡 PowerShell survival tips — these alone would have saved me three errors: (1) Use a normal window, not “Run as administrator”. If your prompt starts with C:\Windows\system32>, it’s an admin window. (2) Copy only the command — never the PS C:\…> prompt in front of it. (3) After installing anything, close PowerShell and open a new window.

Part 1 — OutSystems 11

Here’s the whole O11 setup in 30 seconds. The steps below explain each line.

Step 1: Install Claude Code

irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex

The installer finished fine — then claude --version said "claude is not recognized". The installer had warned me, in yellow, that its folder wasn't in my PATH. One command fixes it:

[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path", [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path","User") + ";$env:USERPROFILE\.local\bin", "User")

Close PowerShell, open a new window, and claude --version prints a version number.

Step 2: Install the OutSystems skill

A skill is a set of instructions that teaches Claude how to use OutSystems’ tools properly. You download it from GitHub — which needs Git. I didn’t have Git, so every command after git clone failed in a chain reaction. Install it first:

winget install --id Git.Git -e --source winget

New window, then:

cd $HOME
git clone https://github.com/OutSystems/outsystems11-mcp.git
cd outsystems11-mcp
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\install.ps1 -Source .
Tip: -Source . matters. Without it, the script ignores your download and fetches a fresh copy from GitHub.

Check it worked — this should print True:

Test-Path "$env:USERPROFILE\.claude\skills\servicestudio-mcp-oml\SKILL.md"

Step 3: Start the MCP server in Service Studio

  1. Open Service Studio and your dev/test module.
  2. Edit → MCP Configuration…
  3. Click Start MCP Server. Leave “automatic merge and publish” off.
  4. Click Copy next to the Claude Code command.

The server does not start by itself — you’ll click this button every time you open Service Studio.

Step 4: Connect Claude to it

Paste the command you copied (it already has the right port):

claude mcp add --transport http servicestudio http://127.0.0.1:41820/mcp --scope user
claude mcp list

You want to see servicestudio: ... √ Connected.

Step 5: Start Claude from your requirements folder

Setup docs often show cd "C:\path\to\your\extracted\requirements-folder". I pasted it literally. Don't — it's a placeholder. Use your real folder:

Expand-Archive "$HOME\Downloads\MyApp.zip" -DestinationPath "$HOME\Downloads\MyApp" -Force
cd "$HOME\Downloads\MyApp"
claude

On first run Claude asks for a theme, your login (it opens the browser), and whether you trust the folder. Then:

  1. Type /mcp — servicestudio should be connected.
  2. Ask: “Summarize the module open in Service Studio. Do not modify anything.”
  3. Switch to Service Studio and click allow on the “allow this agent?” prompt.

If you get a summary of your module back — you’re connected. 🎉

Prefer the desktop app over PowerShell?

Once the steps above are done, open the Claude desktop app → Code → start a local session → pick your requirements folder. It’s the same engine with a friendlier window, and servicestudio is already there.

One catch: normal cloud chats can’t reach O11, because Service Studio only listens on your own PC (127.0.0.1). Use a local Code session.

How changes reach your module

Claude never edits your module directly. It prepares the change, Service Studio opens Compare-and-Merge, and you accept or reject it. Then you publish yourself. That review step is the safety net — keep it.

Part 2 — OutSystems Developer Cloud (ODC)

ODC is easier: there’s nothing to start in a studio, and one plugin installs both the connection and the skills. You’ll need Claude Code from Part 1, Step 1.

Option A: PowerShell (the path OutSystems tests)

Replace acme.outsystems.dev with your tenant — host only, no https://:

claude plugin marketplace add OutSystems/outsystems-mcp
claude plugin install outsystems@outsystems --config tenant_hostname=acme.outsystems.dev
claude mcp list

You’ll see plugin:outsystems:outsystems ... ! Needs authentication. I thought something had broken. It hadn't — you just haven't signed in yet:

  1. Run claude.
  2. Type /mcp, select plugin:outsystems:outsystems, choose Authenticate.
  3. Sign in with your ODC account in the browser that opens.
  4. Ask: “In ODC, which environments do I have?”

Option B: the Claude desktop app (Chat, Cowork and Code)

My first idea was Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector. Skip it — OutSystems documents that it always fails at sign-in, because ODC only accepts sign-ins that return to your own PC.

I also noticed the plugin from Option A didn’t show up in the desktop app’s Code tab. The fix is a tiny local proxy called mcp-remote.

1. Install Node.js and the proxy

winget install OpenJS.NodeJS.LTS

New window, then:

npm.cmd install -g mcp-remote@0.14.3
Why npm.cmd? On my work laptop, plain npx failed with “running scripts is disabled on this system”. The .cmd versions aren’t blocked. And use exactly 0.14.3 — OutSystems notes that versions 0.9.0 to 0.13.5 fail every sign-in.

2. Add ODC to the app’s config

In the desktop app: Settings → Developer → Edit Config. My file had no mcpServers section, so I added one as the first key and left everything else alone:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "outsystems": {
      "command": "cmd",
      "args": ["/c", "npx mcp-remote@0.14.3 https://acme.outsystems.dev/mcp"]
    }
  },
  "...your existing settings...": "stay as they are"
}

3. Quit fully and reopen

Right-click the Claude icon in the system tray → Quit. Closing the window isn’t enough. Then start a new chat and ask “In ODC, list my apps” — the browser opens for sign-in.

4. (Recommended) add the plugin’s rules

The proxy gives Claude the tools; the plugin gives it the rules, like confirm before publish or deploy. Install the outsystems plugin from the OutSystems/outsystems-mcp marketplace in the desktop app's plugin settings.

More stages? More tenants?

Stages (Dev, QA, Prod) need nothing extra — one connection covers them all. Just say which one: “deploy MyApp from Development to QA”.

Another tenant needs its own entry. In the desktop config, add a second block with a different name:

"outsystems-clienta": {
  "command": "cmd",
  "args": ["/c", "npx mcp-remote@0.14.3 https://clienta.outsystems.dev/mcp"]
}

In PowerShell, keep one folder per tenant so you can’t hit the wrong one:

claude mcp add --transport http odc-clienta https://clienta.outsystems.dev/mcp --scope project
Gotcha: after adding a tenant, an old chat still couldn’t see it. Chats load their servers when they start — open a new chat.

The errors cheat sheet

Every one of these happened to me. Bookmark it.

Prompts that worked for me

Start read-only. Always.

Summarize the module open in Service Studio. List its entities, screens and actions. Do not modify anything.

Build from a requirements folder (run Claude inside that folder):

Using the requirements and designs in this folder as the source of truth, implement the app in the module open in Service Studio. Inspect the module first and reuse what exists. Work in small batches and open each change in Compare-and-Merge for my review. Ask only about decisions that could lose data. Don't publish. At the end, list what's done and what's missing.

If Claude stops at a plan:

Don't stop at planning. Re-read the module, list what's still missing, and continue implementing it with the MCP tools.

With both platforms connected, start every prompt with “In ODC…” or “In O11…”. OutSystems’ rules tell Claude not to guess — and you don’t want it to.

Five safety rules I now follow

  1. Dev/test only. Never connect Claude to a production module or stage without a human review.
  2. Keep the review step. O11’s Compare-and-Merge and ODC’s publish/deploy confirmations are your safety net. Don’t auto-approve the tools that change things.
  3. Claude acts as you. In ODC every call uses your roles and lands in the audit trail.
  4. Publish before a break (ODC). Idle Mentor sessions close and throw away unpublished edits.
  5. No secrets in prompts or requirement folders. No passwords, no tokens, no real customer data.

Wrapping up

The first setup took me an evening, mostly spent on errors that now take one line to fix. With this guide it should take you about 30 minutes for both platforms.

The payoff is real: asking “walk me through what this module does” or “list every app deployed in QA” and getting a precise answer in seconds changes how you work with an OutSystems estate.

If this saved you an evening, give it a clap 👏 and share it with your team. Hit a different error? Drop it in the comments and I’ll add it to the cheat sheet.

Resources

  • OutSystems 11 MCP on GitHub
  • OutSystems MCP for ODC on GitHub
  • OutSystems MCP — ODC documentation
  • Model Context Protocol

O11 model writes are a Beta feature at OutSystems; behaviour may change between Service Studio releases. Recordings in this post are illustrative and use placeholder names.

medium.titulo: Nuxt 的檔案式路由，pages 裡放一個檔案，就能產生網址
medium.resumo: 只要在 pages/ 資料夾裡面新增一個 .vue 檔案
medium.conteudo_html:
只要在 pages/ 資料夾裡面新增一個 .vue 檔案

Nuxt 就能自動產生對應的頁面路由

以前學 Vue 或 Angular 時，多少都有接觸過路由設定

但 Nuxt 這種方式讓我覺得很不一樣

為什麼只是新增一個檔案，Nuxt 就知道它對應哪個網址

什麼是 Routing

Routing（路由），簡單來說，就是決定使用者進入某個網址時，應該顯示哪個頁面。

一個電影網站：

  • /：首頁
  • /movies：電影列表
  • /about：關於我們

一般使用 Vue Router 時，我們可以自行設定網址與 Component 的對應關係。

const routes = [
  {
    path: '/movies',
    component: MovieList
  }
]

意思是當使用者進入 /movies，就顯示 MovieList 這個元件。

但 Nuxt 幫我們省去了許多手動設定的工作。

Nuxt 的檔案式路由

Nuxt 有一個功能叫做 File-based Routing 檔案式路由

只要在 pages/ 裡面建立對應的 Vue 檔案

就能依照檔案結構自動建立路由

pages/
  index.vue
  about.vue
  movies/
    index.vue
    popular.vue

Nuxt 會依照預設規則產生：

pages/index.vue
就是 /

pages/about.vue
就是 /about

pages/movies/index.vue
就是 /movies

pages/movies/popular.vue
就是 /movies/popular

Nuxt 不是每次有人輸入網址，才去資料夾裡尋找檔案

而是在開發或建置應用程式時，掃描 pages/ 裡面的檔案，依照命名規則自動產生 Vue Router 的路由設定

所以我們不用每新增一個頁面，就自己寫一次路由對照表

index.vue 代表該層路徑的預設頁面

因此 pages/index.vue 對應 /

而 pages/movies/index.vue 對應 /movies

網址裡面的內容會改變

假設電影網站有幾千部電影

難道要為每部電影建立一個 Vue 檔案嗎？

當然不用。

Nuxt 提供了 Dynamic Routes 動態路由。

pages/
  movies/
    index.vue
    [id].vue

其中 [id].vue 的 id 是一個可以變動的路由參數。

因此以下網址，都能對應到同一個頁面元件：

/movies/100
/movies/200
/movies/300

那要怎麼知道使用者目前選擇哪部電影？

可以使用 useRoute()：

<script setup>
const route = useRoute()
const movieId = route.params.id
</script>

<template>
  <h1>電影編號：{{ movieId }}</h1>
</template>

假設使用者進入：

/movies/100

那麼 route.params.id 就會取得 "100"。

之後就可以根據這個 ID，向 API 查詢對應的電影資料。

路由負責決定顯示哪個頁面，以及提供網址參數

但不代表它會自動幫我們查詢資料。

NuxtPage 又是做什麼

了解路由怎麼產生後，還有一個問題。

Nuxt 知道 /movies 對應哪個頁面，但它要把頁面顯示在哪裡？

這時就會用到 <NuxtPage />。

例如在 app.vue 中：

<template>
  <NuxtPage />
</template>

可以把它想成一個放置目前頁面的容器。

當使用者進入 /movies，Nuxt Router 就會根據路由設定，讓對應的頁面元件顯示在這個位置。

如果想要在網站裡切換頁面，也可以使用 Nuxt 提供的 <NuxtLink>：

<NuxtLink to="/movies">
  查看電影列表
</NuxtLink>

點擊後，就能在應用程式中導向電影列表頁面。

重點整理

  • Routing（路由）：決定網址要對應哪個頁面。
  • File-based Routing（檔案式路由）：Nuxt 根據 pages/ 的檔案結構，自動產生路由設定。
  • index.vue：代表該資料夾層級的預設頁面。
  • Dynamic Routes（動態路由）：使用 [id].vue 等檔名，讓不同的網址參數共用同一個頁面元件。
  • useRoute()：取得目前的路由資訊，例如網址參數。
  • NuxtPage：顯示目前路由對應的頁面元件。
  • NuxtLink：在 Nuxt 應用程式中進行頁面導航。

流程

  • Nuxt 掃描 pages/
  • 自動產生路由設定
  • Vue Router 比對網址
  • NuxtPage 顯示對應的頁面

medium.titulo: Hardening Vue.js: Advanced Security Frameworks for Frontend Engineers (2026)
medium.resumo: The ubiquity of modern reactive frameworks has shifted a massive amount of business logic to the client side. While Vue.js is inherently…
medium.conteudo_html:
The ubiquity of modern reactive frameworks has shifted a massive amount of business logic to the client side. While Vue.js is inherently secure out of the box — leveraging automatic HTML escaping under the hood — it is not bulletproof.

As applications grow in architectural complexity, developers often bypass built-in guardrails for the sake of flexibility, inadvertently opening the door to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), Component Injection, and State Mutation Vulnerabilities.

For frontend engineers, securing an application isn’t just a devops or backend responsibility; it starts at the component layer. Here is a technical breakdown of critical vulnerabilities in Vue.js applications and the precise engineering patterns required to mitigate them.

1. Eliminating XSS in Dynamic Rendering

Vue’s template syntax {{ }} automatically escapes HTML entities, making generic XSS attacks difficult to execute. However, vulnerabilities frequently arise when developers use the v-html directive to render rich text or user-generated content.

<!-- THE VULNERABILITY -->
<div v-html="userProvidedBio"></div>

If userProvidedBio contains an payload like <img src=x onerror=alert(1)>, it executes immediately in the user's browser context.

The Technical Mitigation:

Never trust raw inputs. If you must render dynamic HTML, you must sanitize the payload before it hits the DOM node using a dedicated library like DOMPurify.

// THE MITIGATION STRATEGY
import DOMPurify from 'dompurify';

export default {
  props: {
    rawContent: { type: String, required: true }
  },
  computed: {
    sanitizedContent(): string {
      return DOMPurify.sanitize(this.rawContent, {
        ALLOWED_TAGS: ['b', 'i', 'em', 'strong', 'a'],
        ALLOWED_ATTR: ['href', 'target']
      });
    }
  }
}
  • Architectural Rule: Enforce strict linting configurations via eslint-plugin-vue to flag any un-sanitized use of v-html across your codebase.

2. Preventing Explicit Injection via Global Properties

In highly modular codebases, developers often pass configurations or methods globally using provide and inject. If these components allow the modification of root instances without type safety or schema validation, malicious actors can manipulate your component’s internal logic via devtools or prototype pollution.

The Code Pattern: Type-Safe and Immutable Injection

Instead of injecting generic strings or objects, use Vue’s InjectionKey coupled with TypeScript to guarantee structural contract adherence and prevent runtime tampering.

// symbols.ts - Defining Type-Safe Keys
import type { InjectionKey, Ref } from 'vue';

export interface UserContext {
  id: string;
  role: 'admin' | 'user';
  updateRole: (newRole: 'admin' | 'user') => void;
}

export const UserContextKey: InjectionKey<Ref<UserContext>> = Symbol('UserContext');

When providing data down the component tree, use readonly wrappers to ensure child components cannot directly mutate state variables without going through an authorized action method.

// ParentComponent.vue
import { provide, ref, readonly } from 'vue';
import { UserContextKey } from './symbols';

const state = ref({
  id: 'usr_0912',
  role: 'user'
});

// Provide a read-only instance to protect the state tree
provide(UserContextKey, readonly(state));

3. Securing Vue Router Navigation Guards

Client-side routing dictates the access control model of your Single Page Application (SPA). A common mistake is relying purely on component metadata (meta.requiresAuth) without verifying cryptographic tokens or checking backend session consistency.

The Advanced Route Guard Implementation:

Always resolve tokens, validate expirations via JWT payload checking, and secure matching rules before resolving the next transition hook.

// router/index.ts
import { createRouter, createWebHistory } from 'vue-router';
import { useAuthStore } from '@/stores/auth';

const router = createRouter({
  history: createWebHistory(),
  routes: [
    {
      path: '/admin/dashboard',
      component: () => import('@/views/AdminDashboard.vue'),
      meta: { requiresAuth: true, allowedRoles: ['admin'] }
    }
  ]
});

router.beforeEach(async (to, from, next) => {
  const authStore = useAuthStore();
  
  if (to.meta.requiresAuth) {
    // 1. Check for client-side token presence
    if (!authStore.isAuthenticated) {
      return next({ path: '/login', query: { redirect: to.fullPath } });
    }
    
    // 2. Validate role requirements against the encrypted token payload
    const userRole = authStore.userRole;
    const allowedRoles = to.meta.allowedRoles as string[];
    
    if (allowedRoles && !allowedRoles.includes(userRole)) {
      return next({ path: '/unauthorized' });
    }
  }
  
  next();
});

4. Mitigating SSR Hydration Discrepancies and XSS (Nuxt Context)

If you are using Server-Side Rendering (SSR) via Nuxt, hydration mismatches can expose dangerous cross-site entry points. When the server state is serialized and sent to the client, it is frequently embedded inside a <script> block.

<!-- VULNERABLE INITIAL STATE SERIALIZATION -->
<script>window.__NUXT__={data: { payload: "${userInput}" }}</script>

If the server does not properly escape characters like </script><script>alert(1)</script>, the client browser parses this text node as a distinct script tag, bypassing standard Content Security Policies (CSP).

The Fix:

Ensure your deployment runtime uses modern sanitization engines like devalue or native template compilers that explicitly escape data payloads passed to useState() hooks.

The Bottom Line: Implement a Zero-Trust Frontend Architecture

Security in a Vue.js application is a process of constant layer verification. The golden rules of production-grade frontend engineering remain absolute:

  • Sanitize every dynamic node (v-html) using trusted tools like DOMPurify.
  • Enforce immutability across your reactive state containers using readonly flags.
  • Implement a strict Content Security Policy (CSP) at the HTTP response header layer to block unauthorized script execution even if an injection occurs.

By designing your code footprint under the assumption that all client-side inputs can be modified, you eliminate vulnerabilities before they reach the server gateway.

corrida_no_ar.titulo: 5 TÊNIS com PLACA DE CARBONO que eu estou gostando de usar
corrida_no_ar.resumo: Conheça os cinco tênis com placa de carbono favoritos do momento, tire dúvidas sobre a Black Friday Run da Velocità, veja medalhas gigantes, um novo recorde mundial master e a primeira mandala numerada do Circuito Brasil Gigante, que será entregue na Maratona de Aracaju.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Terça-feira | 27 de outubro de 2026

Neste episódio, Sérgio Rocha apresentou os cinco tênis com placa de carbono que mais tem gostado de usar nos treinos. Sem entrar em detalhes técnicos aprofundados, ele mostrou os modelos que se destacaram em sua rotação:

• “Qiaodan Feiying Plaid 3.0:” Após não gostar da versão 2.0, Sérgio comemorou o retorno da qualidade da linha Plaid. Ele destacou o design, o conforto proporcionado pela língua acolchoada e o visual que deixa a placa de carbono à mostra. O modelo custa R$ 1.399,00.

• “Skechers Aero Elite:” O primeiro supertênis da Skechers impressionou pela responsividade e maciez, sendo comparado ao Puma Fast-R. Apesar de um pouco instável no calcanhar, é uma ótima opção para corredores com boa técnica. Custa R$ 1.649,00.

• “Brooks Hyperion Elite 6:” Com lançamento previsto para 4 de novembro no Brasil, o tênis se mostrou muito equilibrado, responsivo e estável. Um dos destaques é o “bigodinho” no calcanhar, com apliques de silicone para um ajuste mais seguro.

• “Kiprun Kipstorm Elite:” O modelo da Decathlon é um pouco mais firme, mas muito agradável de correr. Com construção em formato de botinha e drop de 5 mm, é uma opção consistente. O valor é de R$ 1.499,00.

• “Hoka Cielo X1 3.0:” Considerado um dos preferidos de Sérgio, a terceira versão do Cielo X1 voltou a ser um tênis excelente e super responsivo, resgatando as qualidades da primeira edição. O preço é de R$ 2.499,00.

Tire suas dúvidas sobre a Black Friday Run da Velocità

A Black Friday Run da Velocità está chegando, e Bruno, da loja, tirou algumas dúvidas frequentes sobre o evento. A corrida acontece no dia 30 de outubro, e cada quilômetro corrido se converte em 1% de desconto, com um limite de 42%. Confira as regras:

• A corrida deve ser feita ao ar livre, pois os dados de GPS são necessários para validação. Treinos na esteira não são válidos.

• Caminhada e corrida contam para a distância, mas o uso de qualquer meio de transporte (bicicleta, patinete, metrô) resultará em banimento.

• Se fizer mais de um treino no dia, apenas a atividade de maior distância será considerada.

• O cupom de desconto é válido para a compra de um único produto, exceto eletrônicos e acessórios de eletrônicos.

• Para evitar atividades duplicadas, quem correr junto com outra pessoa deve iniciar o treino em horários ligeiramente diferentes ou alterar o percurso para que os registros não fiquem idênticos.

As medalhas gigantes da Mountain Do

O Mountain Do é conhecido por suas experiências únicas e, claro, por suas medalhas impressionantes. Foram exibidas as peças gigantescas de algumas das etapas mais icônicas: Costão do Santinho, Fim del Mundo (Ushuaia), Deserto do Saara e Selva Amazônica. Recorde mundial para os 50+ na Maratona de Frankfurt
